entities.summary:
Pierre Desprès (c. 1288 – May 24, 1361) emerged as a formidable French cardinal and diplomat during the turbulent Avignon Papacy, serving under Popes John XXII, Benedict XII, Clement VI, and Innocent VI. His career spanned over four decades, placing him at the nexus of ecclesiastical administration, legal reform, and international diplomacy during a period marked by profound challenges to papal authority, the Hundred Years' War, and the devastating Black Death. As a leading figure in the papal curia, Desprès played a crucial role in shaping the Church's response to political pressures from European monarchs and internal schisms, solidifying the administrative and financial structures of the Avignon pontificate.

Elevated to Cardinal-Priest of Santa Pudenziana in 1327 by Pope John XXII, and then Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina in 1331, Desprès's influence grew steadily. He served as Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church from 1325 until his death, a position of immense power overseeing the papal chancery, which processed all official papal documents and correspondence. He was instrumental in the canonical process for the canonization of Thomas Aquinas under John XXII in 1323 and later became Dean of the Sacred College of Cardinals in 1354. His diplomatic efforts included significant legations, such as negotiating peace between England and France during the early stages of the Hundred Years' War, although often without lasting success due to the entrenched conflict.

entities.summary:
Pierre Desprès (1288–1361) was a French Cardinal during the period of the Avignon Papacy. As a key figure in the Catholic Church during the 14th century, he played a significant role in shaping the religious landscape of Western Europe. Born in France around 1280, Pierre Desprès rose through the ranks of the clergy and became a prominent advisor to Pope Urban V, who succeeded John XXII as the head of the Catholic Church in 1362.

Desprès's contributions to the Church were not limited to his political influence; he also made significant strides in the realm of canon law. His work on the Decretum Gratiani, a foundational text of medieval canon law, helped establish the principles that would guide the development of Catholic doctrine for centuries to come.

Despite his many accomplishments, Desprès's legacy is not without controversy. Some historians have criticized him for his alleged involvement in the sale of indulgences, which contributed to the widespread corruption and abuse of power within the Church during the 14th century.

Today, Pierre Desprès is remembered as a complex figure who played a pivotal role in shaping the course of Western European history. His contributions to the Catholic Church continue to influence the development of Christian doctrine and practice to this day.
